title: The snake's gait
hookLine: the next stanzas move in a meter named for a snake's gliding motion
last: KARAM NAAM — MERCY HERE, PROTECTION THERE.

lines: A RHYTHM NAMED FOR THAT MOTION.
cards: Watch a snake cross a path. It doesn't step. It doesn't hop.

It pours. A small ripple starts at the head and travels down the whole body, and the snake is somewhere else before you've decided whether to be scared. No jerks, no pauses, one smooth wave after another.
Indian poets heard that motion in certain rhythms of words, and they named one meter for it. When Jaap Sahib leaves its first stanza, it starts to move exactly like that.

teach.b: The meter is called bhujang prayat. Bhujang is a snake; prayat means going, moving. The snake's gait.
It's an old meter of Sanskrit poetry, and Guru Gobind Singh uses it for long stretches of Jaap.

teach.h: SHORT, LONG, LONG: ONE SMALL WAVE.
teach.b: It's built from little groups of three syllables, and every group goes the same way: short, long, long. Da, DUM, DUM. Listen to the opening of the second stanza: na-mas-tvam, a-kaa-le.
Short, long, long. Short, long, long.
Then: na-mas-tvam, kri-paa-le. And: na-mas-tvam, a-roo-pe. Then: na-mas-tvam, a-noo-pe.

Once you hear it, you can't stop hearing it. Each group is a small wave, and the waves keep rolling, line after line, the way a snake's body carries one ripple into the next. Why does rhythm matter in a prayer?

Because Jaap is meant to be said out loud, often fast, often from memory, often by a whole room together. A steady meter lets a whole room glide through salutation after salutation without losing its place.
The rhythm carries the words, so the mind is free to carry the meaning. And that ends the week. A few days ago you stood at the lookout.
Since then: Jaap, the Tenth Guru's morning praise; the One with no mark and no caste; the king of kings above every throne; and the names drawn from deeds.
Now the hymn begins to glide.

how: Sikhs recite the bhujang prayat stanzas of Jaap Sahib in a steady, rolling rhythm, often quickly and from memory, and in a group the shared meter keeps everyone together.

o: a yoga pose that copies a rising cobra
a gliding meter of short, long, long beats
a dance done at weddings in the Punjab

practice: Say four lines slowly, tapping your knee on each long syllable: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, namastvam aroope, namastvam anoope.

Say them once more, a little faster, and let them run together like one long wave; the meaning comes over the next few days. Then stop, and let your breath find its own smooth rhythm, no jerks, no pauses.
